title: “KISS ME WITH THE KISSES OF HIS MOUTH”: WHY DOES THE BIBLE OPEN A LOVE SONG LIKE THIS?
paragraphs: “KISS ME WITH THE KISSES OF HIS MOUTH”: WHY DOES THE BIBLE OPEN A LOVE SONG LIKE THIS?

The first sentence of the Song of Songs sounds almost too intimate to be Scripture. But perhaps what makes us uncomfortable is exactly what exposes how little we understand about holy love—and how desperately the human heart was created to be fully known, faithfully loved, and ultimately redeemed.
“Kiss me with the kisses of his mouth…”
Wait.
That is in the Bible?
Not buried somewhere in an obscure manuscript. Not hidden behind a theological metaphor. Not something added by a modern writer trying to make Scripture provocative.
It is essentially how the Song of Songs begins.

Before we sanitize it, spiritualize it, turn it into a sermon illustration, or rush past it because it makes respectable Christians slightly uncomfortable, we need to hear what the Hebrew actually says.
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ
Yishaqēnî minnĕshîqôth pîhû.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.”
Then:
כִּי־טוֹבִים דֹּדֶיךָ מִיָּיִן
Kî-tôvîm dōdeykhā miyyāyin.
“For your love is better than wine.”
Song of Songs 1:2.
There is no need to make the Hebrew less intimate than it is.
The woman desires the man she loves.
She speaks first.
She longs for his kiss.
And God allowed those words into Holy Scripture.
That alone should make us pay attention.
Because perhaps one of our problems is that we have sometimes confused holiness with emotional coldness.
We imagine that anything deeply passionate must somehow be less spiritual.
But the Bible does not begin the Song of Songs with two detached people discussing abstract principles of romance.
It begins with longing.
Desire.
Anticipation.
A woman who does not merely want to know that she is loved intellectually.
She wants love brought near.
“Kiss me…”
There is something painfully human about that sentence.
Because beneath all the things we spend our lives chasing, there remains a hunger most of us rarely admit aloud.
We want to be wanted.
Not tolerated.
Not merely useful.
Not noticed only when somebody needs something.
Wanted.
Known without being discarded.
Seen without being abandoned.
Loved without having to perform every second to keep that love alive.
Maybe that is why these ancient words still feel strangely modern.
You can have thousands of Facebook friends and still wonder whether anybody actually knows you.
You can sleep beside someone and feel miles away.
You can sit in church surrounded by worshippers while privately wondering whether God has become tired of you.
You can smile for the photograph.
Post the Bible verse.
Say, “God is good.”
Answer, “I’m blessed.”
And still carry a silent question underneath all of it:
Does anybody really love the person underneath this version of me?
Song of Songs begins where many of us are afraid to begin.
With desire.
But we need to understand the book carefully.

The Song of Songs is genuine love poetry. Its language celebrates the attraction, delight, exclusivity, longing, beauty, and covenantal dimensions of human love. We do not honor Scripture by pretending the man and woman are not actually speaking about one another.
The kisses are kisses.
The attraction is real.
The poetry is intentionally intimate.
God is not embarrassed by the love He designed.
Yet Christians throughout history have also heard something deeper echoing through this biblical portrait of faithful love.
Not because every romantic sentence should automatically be converted into a secret code about Jesus.
That would flatten the actual poetry.
Rather, because the whole biblical story eventually reveals a mystery larger than any human romance.
Marriage itself can point beyond itself.
Paul writes that a husband and wife becoming “one flesh” carries a profound mystery, and he connects that mystery to Christ and the church in Ephesians 5:31–32.
That changes how Christians can hear the Song.
The Song is not transformed into a decoder ring where every kiss, fragrance, garden, breast, spice, and vineyard must have an invented spiritual equivalent.
But neither must Christian readers stop at human romance.
Human covenant love can become a window.
And beyond that window stands the Bridegroom.
Jesus Christ.
Suddenly the deepest ache beneath the poetry becomes familiar.
Because Scripture tells another love story.
One far more scandalous.
Except in this story, the Bride was not spotless.
We were not waiting beautifully in a garden, deserving to be pursued.
We ran.
We rebelled.
We sinned.
We hid.
Humanity's oldest instinct after sin was not to run toward God.
It was to hide from Him.
Adam and Eve heard God walking in the garden and concealed themselves.
And we have been sewing fig leaves ever since.
Different leaves.
Same hiding.
Success.
Religion.
Money.
Sex.
Achievement.
Entertainment.
Ministry.
Busyness.
Relationships.
Followers.
Reputation.
Even theological knowledge can become another leaf if we use knowledge about God to avoid surrendering ourselves to God.
We desperately want intimacy while simultaneously fearing what intimacy requires:
being known.
That is the terrifying contradiction inside the human heart.
“Love me…”
But don't look too closely.
“Come near…”
But not near enough to discover what I did.
“Know me…”
But only the version I have carefully prepared for you.
And then comes Jesus.
Not merely offering advice from heaven.
Coming near.
“The Word became flesh, and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).
Think about that.
The God humanity ran from became flesh and entered the neighborhood of the fugitives.
He touched lepers.
He ate with sinners.
He received the disgraced.
He spoke with people respectable society preferred to avoid.
He let a woman with a shattered reputation weep at His feet.
He restored failures.
He confronted hypocrites.
He welcomed children.
He called sinners to repentance.
He did not redefine darkness as light to make people comfortable.
He stepped into our darkness to bring us into His light.
That distinction matters.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God doing what sinners could never do to rescue us from what sin has done.
And the cross proves the cost.
This is where the love story becomes almost unbearable.
The One who never sinned was betrayed with a kiss.
A kiss.
Judas approached Jesus in Gethsemane and used an act normally associated with affection as the signal of betrayal.
Imagine the contrast.
Song of Songs opens with:
“Let him kiss me…”
The Gospels move toward a garden where the Son of God receives a traitor's kiss.
Human love longs for intimacy.
Human sin corrupts even intimacy.
And Jesus walks straight through our corruption toward the cross.
He knows what counterfeit affection feels like.
He knows the difference between lips that approach Him and hearts that belong to Him.
That should disturb every comfortable Christian.
Because it is possible to sing His name without surrendering to Him.
It is possible to post Scripture while privately feeding the sin Scripture condemns.
It is possible to say “Lord” publicly while protecting an idol privately.
Judas was physically close enough to kiss Jesus.
And still infinitely far from Him in his heart.
So perhaps the frightening question is not simply:
“Do I believe in Jesus?”
Perhaps tonight the question becomes:
Have I merely learned how to stay close enough to Christianity to look faithful while keeping Jesus away from the rooms in my heart I refuse to surrender?
That secret addiction.
That bitterness.
That relationship you know is dragging you from God.
That pornography nobody knows about.
That affair living first in messages and imagination.
That pride dressed like discernment.
That unforgiveness you have renamed “boundaries” when what you really mean is hatred.
That hunger for approval.
That hidden dishonesty.
That carefully maintained Christian image.
You can fool an audience.
You cannot fool Christ.
And strangely, that is not only terrifying.
It is beautiful.
Because the Jesus who already knows the truth about you is the same Jesus who calls sinners to come.
You do not have to clean yourself into acceptability before approaching the cross.
You come confessing that you cannot clean yourself.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
That is Gospel.
Not pretending.
Not image management.
Not religious cosmetics.
Repentance.
Grace.
Forgiveness.
New life.
The Bridegroom does not merely make sinful people feel better about remaining chained.
He breaks chains.
He calls the dead to life.
He forgives the guilty.
He cleanses the stained.
He restores the broken.
He teaches people who spent their lives searching for love in destructive places what love actually is.
And perhaps now we understand why Song of Songs can hurt so beautifully.
“For your love is better than wine.”
Wine represented pleasure, celebration, abundance.
Yet the beloved says there is something better.
Your love.
Now carry that longing carefully into the greater biblical story.
How many “wines” have you tasted trying to satisfy something only God could ultimately fill?
Approval tasted good for a moment.
Then you needed another compliment.
Money promised security.
Then you needed more.
Sex promised intimacy.
Without covenant and holiness, it could leave another wound.
Social media promised connection.
Then you found yourself staring at a screen wondering why everyone else's life looked happier.
Success promised significance.
Then yesterday's achievement became today's minimum expectation.
Sin always makes extravagant promises.
Then sends an invoice.
Jesus tells the truth before He asks for your life.
Following Him means denying yourself and taking up your cross.
Repentance may hurt.
Obedience may cost you relationships, habits, opportunities, pleasures, reputations, and versions of yourself you thought you needed.
But Christ does not empty your hands merely to leave them empty.
He calls you from death into life.
From slavery into freedom.
From condemnation into justification.
From estrangement into reconciliation.
From orphan-hearted wandering into adoption.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you have spent years believing your scandal is the final chapter.
Divorce.
Addiction.
Sexual sin.
Abortion.
Infidelity.
Prison.
Failure.
A secret nobody knows.
Something done to you.
Something done by you.
A season when you walked away from God.
A prayer you stopped praying because you became convinced heaven had stopped listening.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
It says Christ is sufficient.
There is a difference.
The cross does not minimize your guilt.
The cross demonstrates how serious sin is—and how astonishing God's mercy is.
Jesus did not bleed because humanity needed motivational content.
He came to save sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And because the tomb is empty, your past does not possess sovereign authority over your future.
Christ does.
Maybe this article reached you while nobody knows what is happening inside you.
Maybe you almost scrolled away.
Maybe that opening sentence about a kiss caught your attention for one reason, but somewhere along the way another sentence found the wound.
If that happened, don't hide now.
You do not need to confess private details publicly.
But you can take one honest step.
And if you cannot find impressive words at all, just write:
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only person fighting their way home.
And somebody needs to hear what you just heard.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because there may be one person among your friends who is smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
You may never know that your share reached them at 2:13 in the morning when temptation was winning.

You may never know that someone opened it after an argument, after falling back into addiction, after considering walking away from their marriage, or after becoming convinced that God could never want them again.
Share it anyway.
There are truths you do not save because you have forgotten them.
You save them because you know there will be a night when you will need to remember them again.
There is another way you can help this work continue.
But hear this carefully.
It does not buy forgiveness.
It does not make God love you more.
And it should never replace faithful generosity to your local church or other responsibilities God has placed before you.
Scripture says giving should not be “grudgingly, or of necessity,” because “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Prayerfully.
Joyfully.
As voluntary support for continuing and expanding Gospel-centered work.

Supporting Christian ministry is biblical; Paul teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their ministry (1 Corinthians 9:14), while Christian generosity must remain willing rather than coerced.
So if you have been asking, “How can I help Gospel Warrior reach more people?” this is one practical answer.
It is mission.
It is another wounded person encountering Scripture.
Another believer being called back from compromise.
Another exhausted Christian remembering grace.
Another seeker hearing clearly that Christianity is not fundamentally about becoming impressive enough for God.
It is about Christ saving sinners who could never save themselves.
Pray.
Share.
Save Gospel-centered resources.
Follow.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the person who does not believe at all but is willing to listen.
Because somewhere beyond your screen is a human being whose polished profile is hiding an aching soul.
And perhaps now we finally understand why the Bible dares to begin this love song with such vulnerable words.
“Kiss me…”
It is the language of nearness.
And underneath so much of human sin is a desperate, disordered search for nearness.
We keep trying to satisfy eternal hunger with temporary things.
Another body.
Another relationship.
Another achievement.
Another purchase.
Another drink.
Another notification.
Another person telling us we matter.
Another distraction so we do not have to sit quietly long enough to hear the emptiness.
Yet Scripture keeps drawing us toward something greater.
Human love is beautiful when received according to God's design.
Marriage is beautiful.
Desire within its holy covenant is beautiful.
A husband delighting in his wife is beautiful.
A wife desiring her husband is beautiful.
God is not embarrassed by any of it.
But even the greatest human love cannot carry the weight of being God.
Your spouse cannot redeem you.
Your boyfriend cannot justify you.
Your girlfriend cannot resurrect you.
Your children cannot become your savior.
Your followers cannot give you eternal life.
Only Christ can bear that weight.
And this is the breathtaking reversal of the Gospel:
We spend our lives crying,
“Someone come close enough to prove I am worth loving.”
Then Jesus Christ comes closer than we imagined…
and shows us something far greater.
Not that we were secretly innocent.
Not that our rebellion never mattered.
Not that every desire we carried was holy.
But that while we were sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8).
He knew.
And came anyway.
He saw the scandal.
And brought grace.
He saw the grave.
And brought resurrection.
He saw what sin had written over your life…
and stepped into history with nail-scarred hands.
So perhaps the deepest question after reading Song of Songs 1:2 is not whether Christians are allowed to talk about kissing.
Perhaps it is this:
What have you been kissing because your soul was starving for a love only God could ultimately give?
Don't answer too quickly.
Sit there.
Let it hurt.
Then bring the answer to Jesus.
Because repentance is not the moment God discovers your scandal.
It is the moment you stop running from the One who already knows—and turn toward the Savior who died and rose to redeem sinners.
Come out of hiding.
Come home.
And remember this when your past whispers your old name tonight:
Your scandal may explain where Jesus found you, but grace gets to tell the world what Jesus did with you.
